Typical use
How it measures
Notes

Flow and Pressure Decide the Choice
Owners often ask which meter fits a building of a certain size. That's the wrong starting question.
Flow rate and operating pressure
drive the choice, because the meter must stay accurate when several appliances run at once on a cold morning.
A
diaphragm meter
suits most homes and small apartments. Inside, flexible diaphragms fill and empty chambers of known volume, and each cycle advances the register. It's a practical, proven design for lower flows.
A
rotary meter

steps up when demand gets heavier, for example in a commercial kitchen where ranges, ovens, and water heating may run together. Two lobes rotate in sequence, moving a fixed amount of gas with each turn.
A
turbine meter

belongs in industrial plants and other large loads. Gas spins a rotor, and faster flow spins it faster. Because turbulence can distort that relationship, it needs a straight run of pipe so the gas arrives in a clean, even stream.

smart meter

isn't defined only by how it senses gas. It adds electronic recording and communication, often by pulse or radio, so readings can be collected remotely and logged more often. California shows how large that shift became. The
California Public Utilities Commission smart meter benefits page
describes authorised programs for
approximately 900,000 natural-gas smart meters
for San Diego Gas & Electric and
approximately 4.2 million
for Pacific Gas and Electric.
How to Identify What You Have
Look at the housing:
Diaphragm meters are the familiar bulky residential units. Rotary and turbine meters look more industrial and sit in line with larger piping.
Look at the face:
Older units use a row of dials. Electronic units show a digital display and may have a radio module attached.
Read the nameplate:
Check the
maximum rated capacity
, serial number, and model before assuming a meter can handle added appliances.
Sizing rule:
An undersized meter can cause pressure loss at peak demand. A smart meter can still fail to report if it doesn't have a usable communications signal.
Use the simple rule first. Diaphragm for most homes, rotary for large commercial loads, turbine for industrial plants, and smart features when remote reading and data logging matter.
How Gas Meters Are Approved and Certified
People often treat approval as one stamp. It's a chain, and confusing the links causes trouble.
Model approval
asks whether the design measures correctly.
Verification
asks whether the individual meter in front of you measures correctly.
The Approval Layers
In Canada,
Measurement Canada administers the Electricity and Gas Inspection Act and approves meter models
. A meter used for billing must carry a valid approval and verification mark. If you're checking what that means for equipment selection, our guide to
Measurement Canada approved meters
explains the approval marks in plain language.

ANSI B109 standards
. State public utility commissions set tariffs and metering rules for utilities, while federal pipeline safety rules under
49 CFR Part 192
cover gas service lines and pressure. Those are different jobs. A safety rule for a service line doesn't prove a meter is accurate, and an accuracy approval doesn't set the tariff.

body.alt: A flowchart explaining the approval and certification process for natural gas meters in Canada.

children.text: Three Checkpoints to Keep Separate
Model approval:
The design is tested before that type of meter is accepted for billing use.
Verification:
The individual unit is checked, often before or at installation, and marked accordingly.
Periodic inspection:
The meter is checked again in service so accuracy does not drift over time.
On the meter body, look for the
verification label or stamp
, the
serial number
, and the relevant date. Photograph all three. If a bill later looks wrong, that photo tells the utility exactly which device supplied the disputed reading.

Start a challenge with facts, not frustration. Ask the utility to test the meter, and include the serial number, the dates in question, and your bill history. Keep your own dated reading photos if you have them. A test can confirm the device, reveal a fault, or show that the error sits elsewhere, for example in an estimated read or a mixed-up account.
Approval confirms the device can measure accurately. It doesn't approve the rate, allocation formula, or common-area split built on top of that measurement.
That last point matters in multi-unit buildings. A perfectly approved master meter can still sit behind an unfair allocation if nobody wrote down how shared gas use is handled.

The Problem a Master Meter Creates

With one master meter, the utility bills the owner for the whole property. The owner then recovers that cost through rent or a separate fee. Residents who use little gas subsidise residents who use a lot, and nobody can see their own signal to conserve.
Unit-level metering assigns each suite its own share. For a plain explanation of the mechanics, see
how submetering works

. The physical requirement comes first, though. Each unit needs its own gas branch, or a meter location that isolates that unit's appliances. Buildings with individual gas heating or rooftop equipment often allow that separation. A single central boiler serving every suite usually doesn't.
Before you allocate anything, separate
common-area loads

. Corridor heating, a shared pool heater, laundry equipment, or a leasing office shouldn't land on tenant bills by accident. Meter those loads separately where practical, or state the allocation rule in writing.
Choose Using Four Decision Points
Who owns the equipment:
Ownership decides who replaces a failed meter and who carries the long-term asset risk.
Who reads it:
Manual reads need access and discipline. Automated collection needs communications that work in the building.
Who issues the bill:
Billing isn't copying a number onto an invoice. Someone must apply rates, handle move-ins, answer questions, and correct errors.
What the tenant agreement says:
Lease language must match the model before billing starts, not after the first complaint.
Match the model to your capacity.
Owner-installed submeters
can suit a small building where staff already handle billing well.
Turnkey submetering
suits a larger property without metering staff, because the provider reads, bills, and maintains the system under agreement. A
hybrid model
fits where suites have individual loads but the property also has shared heating or amenities that belong to the owner.
Tenant Protection Is Part of the Design
Accurate consumption isn't enough if the economics are wrong. A recent
California Public Utilities Commission proceeding
defines a master-metered property as one where a single utility meter serves a customer of record who distributes, submeters, or allocates service among tenants. California Public Utilities Code
requires submetered mobile-home-park residents to be charged the same rates that would apply if the utility served them directly, and requires applicable rebates to be passed through to residents.

Rules differ by place and property type, so don't copy California's rule into another jurisdiction. Do copy its lesson. Ask how utility-equivalent rates, eligible discounts, rebates, customer charges, and move-in or move-out dates will be handled. Get the answer in writing before any model goes live, because the owner carries the duty when the owner stands between the utility and the tenant.
Installation Checklist and Billing Mistakes to Avoid

Most billing problems are installed months before the first invoice. A meter goes on the wrong branch, a start reading isn't recorded, or nobody decides who pays for common areas. Work through the steps in order, with one owner for each.

body.alt: A four-step infographic explaining responsibilities for natural gas meter installation and billing tasks.

children.text: The Ten Step Checklist
Map the gas distribution (owner):
Trace branch lines, supply pressure, and each unit's appliances. A meter can only measure the load downstream of where it sits.
Size to peak demand (provider or engineer):
Include planned appliances, not just today's load. Sizing to average use causes pressure loss in winter when heating, cooking, and hot water overlap.
Confirm permits and a licensed gas fitter (owner):
Gas work isn't general handyman work. If you're preparing for review, guidance on
gas line permits and inspections
helps you understand what inspectors expect before work starts.
Plan isolation and access (fitter):
Coordinate shutoffs and suite entry early. Gas shutoff often takes
one to two days
, so residents need notice that matches the schedule.
Leak test every fitting (fitter):
Test after installation, not after the first smell complaint. Document the result for each disturbed joint.
Verify approvals and record identity (fitter):
Log serial numbers, verification dates, and exact meter locations. A swapped serial number can bill Unit 204 for Unit 304.
Commission the readings (provider):

Record start indexes, then reconcile the sum of unit readings against the master meter. Investigate any gap before billing. A small unexplained difference needs a defined home, not a quiet spread across tenants.
Issue tenant notice and lease language (owner):
Explain when billing starts, the estimate rule for missed reads, and the proration formula for move-ins and move-outs. Our overview of
how to bill tenants for utilities
covers the tenant-facing pieces to settle first.
Set billing rules (owner):
Write down the rate basis, fixed charges, and common-area allocation before the first cycle. A reading alone does not produce a fair bill.
Schedule maintenance and replacement (provider or owner):
Plan for the meters' service life, battery or communications failures where applicable, and periodic accuracy checks.
Where Estimates Go Wrong
Don't let estimates run for months. When the actual read finally arrives, one tenant gets a catch-up bill that looks like a penalty, even if the total gas use was real.

Schedule actual reads on a fixed rhythm and investigate missed reads quickly. If an estimate is unavoidable, label it clearly, state how it was calculated, and say when it will be trued up. Residents accept corrections far better when the method was disclosed before the surprise.

Keep a simple audit file for every unit. It should hold the meter serial number, location, start index, verification details, and the billing rule version in force. When a resident questions a charge, you can walk from the physical meter to the invoice without guessing. That paper trail is the difference between a defensible bill and an argument.

flow and pressure
at peak demand? Second, which
approval and verification mark
applies in your jurisdiction? Third, which submetering model matches who will own the equipment, read it, and bill residents?

Utility bills:
Collect
twelve months
of bills so winter peaks and summer lows are both visible.
Appliance list:
List gas appliances by unit, including heating, hot water, cooking, dryers, and rooftop equipment.
Gas layout drawings:
Bring any drawings you have, even if they're old. They give an assessor a starting map to verify in the field.

Confirm the meters carry the verification mark required in your jurisdiction, and whether the consultation carries any obligation. We offer a free consultation and a free assessment of a building's gas infrastructure, with no obligation.

The best setup isn't the one with the newest meter. It's the one whose billing rules are written down, whose common loads are separated, and whose readings can be traced from a named meter to a named unit.
